doorway: Presents to the family medicine clinic with burning on urination and right-sided back pain.
Vital signs are supplied at this station.
A point-of-care urine dipstick was obtained by the medical assistant before you entered; the result is on the chart.
Perform a focused history and physical examination, and discuss your plan with the patient.

plan.notice: Fever with flank pain and urinary symptoms requires assessment of systemic illness and ability to tolerate fluids.
plan.pivot: Clarify fever and chills, onset, dysuria, vomiting, obstruction history, allergies and pregnancy possibility.
plan.exam: Assess perfusion, abdomen and specific CVA tenderness; the finding supports localization but does not provide a culture or identify an organism.
plan.avoid: Writing a culture result or assigning an organism before testing; missing allergy reaction details.

goals: Ask whether she has been able to keep fluids down since vomiting - it separates outpatient from inpatient management.
Ask directly about back trauma or heavy lifting to make the musculoskeletal differential a real one rather than a placeholder.
Ask what she thinks is going on before offering reassurance - the F.I.F.E. item is a question, not a statement.

timeline.student: Hello, I am a medical student. I will listen to your concerns, examine you with your permission, and discuss the next steps.
timeline.patient: Hello. Thank you for introducing yourself. I am ready to talk.

timeline.student: What brings you in today?
timeline.patient: I've had this burning when I pee for a couple of days, and since yesterday my back has been hurting on the right side. I've been feeling really lousy — I think I have a fever.
timeline.why: Fever with flank pain and urinary symptoms requires assessment of systemic illness and ability to tolerate fluids.

timeline.student: I will arrange urgent help from my supervising clinician now. We will not delay emergency care to finish routine questions.
timeline.patient: Okay, that makes sense.
timeline.why: Stated escalation in a simulation. Continue the remaining example only while care permits; do not delay transfer or stabilization for nonurgent checklist items.

timeline.student: How bad are the symptoms, and how do they affect what you can do?
timeline.patient: The back pain is about a seven out of ten right now — it got up to an eight last night. The burning is maybe a five.
timeline.why: Intensity and functional effect are distinct; record only the dimension answered.

timeline.student: Is the back ache constant, and when does the burning happen?
timeline.patient: The back ache is there all the time. The burning only happens when I actually go.
timeline.why: Separate time since onset from duration of one episode and from continuity.

timeline.student: When did the burning with urination start?
timeline.patient: The burning started about two days ago.
timeline.why: Clarify fever and chills, onset, dysuria, vomiting, obstruction history, allergies and pregnancy possibility.

timeline.student: When did the back pain start?
timeline.patient: The back pain started yesterday, on the right side.
timeline.why: Clarify fever and chills, onset, dysuria, vomiting, obstruction history, allergies and pregnancy possibility.

timeline.student: How have your symptoms changed since they started?
timeline.patient: It started with just the burning. Then yesterday the back pain and the fever came on, and it's been getting worse since.
timeline.why: Change over time can change urgency even when the symptom is familiar.

timeline.student: Where do you feel the symptoms?
timeline.patient: It's right here — the right side of my back, just under my ribs. The burning is lower down, in front, when I go.

timeline.student: Does the discomfort spread anywhere else?
timeline.patient: Sometimes it wraps around toward the front, down near my right hip and groin.
timeline.why: Spread of discomfort can connect an apparent local complaint with another system.

timeline.student: What does it feel like?
timeline.patient: The back pain is like a deep, constant ache. The peeing is more of a burning, stinging feeling.
timeline.why: Use the patient’s words before translating them into a clinical description.

timeline.student: Was there an injury or any trigger you noticed?
timeline.patient: Nothing that I can think of. I didn't hurt my back or fall or anything.

timeline.student: What makes it better?
timeline.patient: Ibuprofen takes the edge off a bit, and a heating pad helps a little.
timeline.why: Relief changes probability, but is not proof that a serious cause is excluded.

timeline.student: What makes it worse?
timeline.patient: Moving around makes it worse. Riding in the car over bumps was awful.
timeline.why: Compare triggers with the chronology; one trigger does not establish a diagnosis.

timeline.student: What have you tried for this, and did it help?
timeline.patient: I've been taking ibuprofen, drinking cranberry juice, and pushing water. It hasn't really fixed it.

timeline.student: Have you had anything like this before?
timeline.patient: I had a bladder infection about six months ago. They gave me antibiotics and it cleared up. But it never got into my back like this.

timeline.student: Have you felt feverish or measured your temperature?
timeline.patient: I've felt hot and sweaty since yesterday. I didn't take my temperature at home.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had shaking chills?
timeline.patient: Yes — I had shaking chills last night under two blankets.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Have you had nausea or vomiting?
timeline.patient: I've been nauseated, and I actually threw up once this morning.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: How often are you urinating?
timeline.patient: I'm going way more often than normal — every hour or so, and barely anything comes out.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: Do you get a sudden urge and have to rush to the bathroom?
timeline.patient: When I have to go, I really have to go — it comes on all of a sudden.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.student: What does your urine look and smell like? Have you seen blood?
timeline.patient: It's been cloudy and it smells stronger than usual. I haven't seen any blood in it.
timeline.why: Use this answer to weigh the possibilities described in the reasoning section.

timeline.patient: No, nothing like that. No discharge or itching.

timeline.patient: No, my bowels have been normal.

timeline.patient: No cough, no trouble breathing, no chest pain.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.patient: No rash anywhere, and no headache. My weight is the same and I haven't had night sweats.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.patient: I have not had diarrhea.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: Have you had constipation?
timeline.patient: I have not had constipation.
timeline.why: A targeted negative changes probability; it does not justify unrelated normal statements.

timeline.student: What medical conditions have you been diagnosed with?
timeline.patient: I'm healthy otherwise. No ongoing medical problems — just that bladder infection six months ago.

timeline.student: Have you had any surgeries or hospital admissions?
timeline.patient: I had my wisdom teeth out when I was eighteen. That's it — I've never been in the hospital.

timeline.student: What medicines do you take, including prescriptions, over-the-counter products, and supplements?
timeline.patient: I take a birth control pill every day. And I've been taking ibuprofen — 400 milligrams, a couple of times a day for the last two days.
timeline.why: Name, dose and frequency matter; do not fill in missing details.

timeline.student: Do you have any medication allergies, and what reaction do you have?
timeline.patient: Yes — sulfa drugs. I broke out in hives when I took something with sulfa as a kid.
timeline.why: Distinguish the substance and reaction from a blanket allergy label.

timeline.student: Do you use tobacco or smoke?
timeline.patient: No, I've never smoked.

timeline.student: Do you drink alcohol, and how much?
timeline.patient: I'll have two or three drinks on a weekend, that's about it.

timeline.student: Do you use any recreational drugs?
timeline.patient: No, I don't use any drugs.

timeline.student: What do you do for work?
timeline.patient: I am a graduate student.

timeline.student: Are you sexually active?
timeline.patient: I am sexually active.

timeline.student: Who do you live with?
timeline.patient: I live with my husband off campus.

timeline.student: How many sexual partners do you have, and have you had a new partner?
timeline.patient: I have one male partner, my boyfriend, and no new partners.

timeline.student: What do you use for birth control?
timeline.patient: We use condoms sometimes, not always.

timeline.student: What health problems run in your family?
timeline.patient: My mom is 52 and has high blood pressure. My dad is 55 and has type 2 diabetes. I have one older brother and he's healthy. No kidney problems or stones in my parents or my brother. My aunt — my mom's sister — was on dialysis, but I never really knew what caused it.
timeline.why: Record which relative and the condition; do not infer a family history from patient worry.

timeline.student: When was your last period?
timeline.patient: My last period was 3 weeks ago.
timeline.why: A reported possibility or menstrual date is not a pregnancy-test result.

timeline.student: Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
timeline.patient: I do not think I am pregnant, but it is possible.
timeline.why: A reported possibility or menstrual date is not a pregnancy-test result.

timeline.student: Are your periods regular?
timeline.patient: My periods are regular.
timeline.why: A reported possibility or menstrual date is not a pregnancy-test result.

timeline.student: What worries you most about these symptoms?
timeline.patient: Honestly? I'm scared it's my kidneys. My aunt ended up on dialysis and I keep thinking about that.
timeline.why: FIFE helps connect the clinical plan with this patient’s concern and circumstances.

timeline.student: How is this affecting your school work?
timeline.patient: And I have a big exam on Friday. I can't afford to be sick for that.
timeline.why: FIFE helps connect the clinical plan with this patient’s concern and circumstances.

timeline.student: Thank you for explaining that. I can understand why this is concerning.
timeline.patient: As I mentioned, and I have a big exam on Friday. I can't afford to be sick for that.

timeline.student: May I have your permission to examine you?
timeline.patient: Yes, that's fine. Go ahead.

timeline.action: General appearance
timeline.finding: Young woman who appears uncomfortable, shifting position in the chair. Alert and oriented, in mild distress. Flushed.

timeline.finding: Tachycardic, regular rhythm. S1 and S2 present. No murmurs, rubs or gallops.
timeline.why: The course expects at least four listening posts, on skin.

timeline.finding: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, all fields. Good air movement. No rales, rhonchi or wheezes.

timeline.action: Offer help into the supine position.
timeline.why: Respect the patient’s response; a position change is not a clinical finding by itself.

timeline.why: Auscultation precedes palpation and percussion.

timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.action: Abdominal special tests — cva tenderness, murphy, mcburney, psoas, obturator
timeline.finding: Costovertebral angle tenderness: markedly positive on the RIGHT. Left is non-tender. Murphy sign negative. McBurney point non-tender. Psoas and obturator negative.
timeline.why: Assess perfusion, abdomen and specific CVA tenderness; the finding supports localization but does not provide a culture or identify an organism.

timeline.action: Inspect skin — chest, back, arms, legs
timeline.finding: On the inspected chest, back, arms and legs: no rashes or lesions on the areas inspected.
timeline.why: This specific action releases only the finding shown here. Interpret it with the history; it does not confirm a diagnosis by itself.

timeline.action: Offer help into the seated position.
timeline.why: Respect the patient’s response; a position change is not a clinical finding by itself.

timeline.action: Osteopathic structural screen — thoracic, lumbar
timeline.finding: T10 through L1 on the right: increased paraspinal tissue texture change, tenderness and hypertonicity. T11 is rotated right.
timeline.why: Name the level examined; findings are released by region.

timeline.student: I recommend evaluating a kidney infection because the urinary symptoms are accompanied by fever and flank pain. We should check urine and pregnancy testing and decide whether you can safely drink and take treatment outside the hospital.
timeline.patient: Alright. Thank you for explaining that.
timeline.why: Proposed care, not a record of tests or treatment already completed.

timeline.student: What questions do you have about the next steps?
timeline.patient: Do you think I'm going to have to go to the hospital for this?

timeline.student: Hospital care may be needed if you are unstable, cannot retain fluids or have an obstructed infected kidney. I recommend assessing those risks now before deciding where treatment is safest. We can address your examination plans after that assessment; I cannot promise recovery by a particular day.
timeline.patient: Okay. I can do that.
timeline.why: Answer the concern that was just expressed. Give a defensible recommendation and explain uncertainty; do not promise a diagnosis or recovery before the evidence supports it.

note.S:
CC: Dysuria for 2 days, right flank pain for 1 day.
HPI: 24-year-old woman with worsening constant dull right flank pain just under the ribs, radiating toward groin, 7/10 (8/10 worst); burning on voiding 5/10. Movement/jarring worsen pain; heat/ibuprofen partly help. Fever, shaking chills, nausea, one emesis, frequency, urgency and cloudy malodorous urine; no gross hematuria. Prior bladder infection 6 months ago without flank symptoms. Tried ibuprofen, cranberry juice and fluids. Concerned about kidney damage because aunt required dialysis.
PMH: No chronic conditions. PSH: Wisdom teeth at 18; no admission.
Meds: Oral contraceptive daily; ibuprofen 400 mg a couple times/day for 2 days. Sulfonamides cause hives.
SH: Graduate student; lives with husband off campus; no tobacco/drugs; 2–3 drinks on weekends. One male sexual partner; inconsistent condoms, no new partner. LMP 3 weeks ago, regular; pregnancy possible.
FH: Mother HTN, father diabetes; brother healthy. No known kidney disease/stones in parents/brother; aunt's dialysis cause unknown.
ROS: GU as above, no discharge. GI: nausea/vomiting, no diarrhea/constipation. General: fever/chills, no weight loss. No cough, chest pain, rash or headache.
P: 1. Obtain urine culture/urinalysis, pregnancy test, CBC and BMP; assess intake, perfusion and obstruction/sepsis risk. Clinician to select a renal-tissue-active antibiotic using pregnancy, allergy and resistance data; avoid sulfonamide allergen and nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis. Explain adherence, hydration and urgent deterioration precautions. Emergency evaluation for instability, inability to retain fluids or infected obstruction; otherwise review in 48–72 hours with culture results.

2. Obtain appropriate renal imaging if obstruction is suspected; clinician-directed analgesia/antiemetic and urgent urology input for infected obstruction. Explain that fever with obstruction needs more than hydration.

3. Pregnancy testing and urgent pelvic ultrasound/Doppler if torsion remains suspected; prompt gynecology review without relying on normal Doppler to exclude it. Provide clinician-directed analgesia and explain emergency return for sudden severe pelvic pain.

CC: Dysuria for 2 days, right flank pain for 1 day.
HPI: 24-year-old woman with worsening constant dull right flank pain just under the ribs, radiating toward groin, 7/10 (8/10 worst); burning on voiding 5/10. Movement/jarring worsen pain; heat/ibuprofen partly help. Fever, shaking chills, nausea, one emesis, frequency, urgency and cloudy malodorous urine; no gross hematuria. Prior bladder infection 6 months ago without flank symptoms. Tried ibuprofen, cranberry juice and fluids. Concerned about kidney damage because aunt required dialysis.
PMH: No chronic conditions. PSH: Wisdom teeth at 18; no admission.
Meds: Oral contraceptive daily; ibuprofen 400 mg a couple times/day for 2 days. Sulfonamides cause hives.
SH: Graduate student; lives with husband off campus; no tobacco/drugs; 2–3 drinks on weekends. One male sexual partner; inconsistent condoms, no new partner. LMP 3 weeks ago, regular; pregnancy possible.
FH: Mother HTN, father diabetes; brother healthy. No known kidney disease/stones in parents/brother; aunt's dialysis cause unknown.
ROS: GU as above, no discharge. GI: nausea/vomiting, no diarrhea/constipation. General: fever/chills, no weight loss. No cough, chest pain, rash or headache.
Care needs: I am worried about getting to follow-up and knowing whom to call if I get worse.
P: 1. Obtain urine culture/urinalysis, pregnancy test, CBC and BMP; assess intake, perfusion and obstruction/sepsis risk. Clinician to select a renal-tissue-active antibiotic using pregnancy, allergy and resistance data; avoid sulfonamide allergen and nitrofurantoin for pyelonephritis. Explain adherence, hydration and urgent deterioration precautions. Emergency evaluation for instability, inability to retain fluids or infected obstruction; otherwise review in 48–72 hours with culture results. Confirm transport and a practical contact for deterioration.

2. Obtain appropriate renal imaging if obstruction is suspected; clinician-directed analgesia/antiemetic and urgent urology input for infected obstruction. Explain that fever with obstruction needs more than hydration.

3. Pregnancy testing and urgent pelvic ultrasound/Doppler if torsion remains suspected; prompt gynecology review without relying on normal Doppler to exclude it. Provide clinician-directed analgesia and explain emergency return for sudden severe pelvic pain.

omissions: Ask whether she has been able to keep fluids down since vomiting - it separates outpatient from inpatient management.
Ask directly about back trauma or heavy lifting to make the musculoskeletal differential a real one rather than a placeholder.
Ask what she thinks is going on before offering reassurance - the F.I.F.E. item is a question, not a statement.
Percuss the abdomen as well as palpating it - the Objective rubric expects the area of concern documented across methods.
